topics.title: Computational thinking
topics.intro: Before any code is written, a computer scientist thinks: break the problem down, ignore what doesn’t matter, spot patterns, and write precise steps. Daedalus didn’t build the labyrinth by guessing.
topics.teach: Explain decomposition and abstraction using planning a school trip as the example.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to “decompose” a family task (cooking dinner, packing for a holiday) into smaller steps.
topics.hook: Four pillars: **break it down, leave out what doesn’t matter, spot patterns, write precise steps**.

topics.title: Flowcharts and pseudocode
topics.intro: Algorithms can be drawn as flowcharts or written in pseudocode: structured English that is easy to turn into any programming language. Every algorithm is built from sequence, selection and iteration.
topics.teach: Explain what each flowchart shape means.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to describe the algorithm {she} uses to get ready in the morning, including one decision.
topics.hook: **Oval = start or stop, rectangle = process, diamond = decision, parallelogram = input or output.**

topics.title: Python: variables, data types and operators
topics.intro: A variable is a named box in memory. Python knows the difference between whole numbers (int), decimals (float), text (str) and True/False (bool), and the type changes what operators do: "3" + "4" is "34"!
topics.teach: Explain why input() needs int() around it before you can do maths with the answer.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what 17 // 5 and 17 % 5 give, and why both are useful.
topics.hook: **int, float, str, bool**: whole numbers, decimals, text and True/False.

topics.title: Selection: if, elif and else
topics.intro: Selection lets a program make decisions, like the Oracle answering differently depending on the question. Python checks conditions in order and runs the first one that is True.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between using elif and using several separate if statements.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to write (on paper) an if/elif/else that turns a test score into a grade.
topics.hook: **if, elif, else**: Python takes the first path that is True and skips the rest.

topics.title: Iteration: for and while loops
topics.intro: Loops repeat code. A for loop repeats a set number of times (count-controlled); a while loop repeats until a condition becomes False (condition-controlled). Forget to change the condition and it loops for ever, like Sisyphus and his boulder.
topics.teach: Explain when you would choose a while loop instead of a for loop.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what range(2, 10, 3) produces.
topics.hook: **for = I know how many times; while = keep going until something changes.**

topics.title: Lists, strings and functions
topics.intro: Lists store many values under one name, and strings are really sequences of characters. Both count positions from 0. Functions package up code so it can be reused, which is decomposition in action.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a parameter and a return value.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what "ODYSSEY"[1:4] would give, and why.
topics.hook: **A list starts counting at 0**: the first item is at index 0.

topics.title: Errors, testing and debugging
topics.intro: Every programmer makes errors. Syntax errors stop the code running at all; runtime errors crash it part-way; logic errors are the sneakiest: the program runs but gives the wrong answer. Good testing finds them.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a syntax error and a logic error, with an example of each.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what “boundary” test data would be for a program that accepts ages 11 to 18.
topics.hook: **Syntax error = bad grammar; runtime error = a crash; logic error = the wrong answer.**

topics.title: Searching algorithms
topics.intro: Linear search checks every item in turn. Binary search keeps halving a SORTED list, so it can find one item among a million in about 20 checks. Choosing the right algorithm matters.
topics.teach: Explain why binary search only works on a sorted list.
topics.talk: Play “I’m thinking of a number from 1 to 100” and count how many guesses halving takes.
topics.hook: **Binary search: halve, halve, halve**, but only on a sorted list.

topics.title: Sorting algorithms
topics.intro: Bubble sort swaps neighbours until nothing moves; insertion sort builds a sorted section one item at a time; merge sort splits the list in half again and again, then merges the pieces: divide and conquer.
topics.teach: Explain how one pass of a bubble sort works.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to sort a hand of playing cards using insertion sort, then explain each step.
topics.hook: **Bubble swaps neighbours, insertion slides each item into place, merge splits then merges.**

topics.title: Binary and hexadecimal
topics.intro: Inside a computer, everything is binary: billions of tiny switches that are on (1) or off (0). Hexadecimal is a shorthand programmers use, because one hex digit stands for exactly four bits.
topics.teach: Explain why programmers use hexadecimal instead of long binary numbers.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to count to 15 in binary on {her} fingers.
topics.hook: **Binary place values double**: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.

topics.title: Binary addition, overflow and shifts
topics.intro: Binary addition works like column addition, but 1 + 1 = 10. When an answer is too big for the bits available, an overflow error happens. Shifting the bits left or right multiplies or divides by 2.
topics.teach: Explain what causes an overflow error.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why shifting 00000101 two places left gives 20.
topics.hook: **1 + 1 = 10 in binary**: write 0, carry 1. Shift left to double, shift right to halve.

topics.title: Representing text, images and sound
topics.intro: Text, pictures and music all become binary. Characters use codes like ASCII and Unicode; images are grids of pixels; sound is sampled thousands of times a second. More bits mean better quality, and bigger files.
topics.teach: Explain how colour depth and resolution affect an image’s file size.
topics.talk: Look at the size of a photo on a phone together and work out why it is so big.
topics.hook: **More bits = better quality = bigger file.**

topics.title: Boolean logic and logic gates
topics.intro: Every decision a computer makes comes down to logic gates: AND, OR, NOT and XOR, built from transistors. A truth table lists every possible input and the output it gives.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between OR and XOR with a real-life example.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to make up a rule for opening a door that needs an AND and a NOT.
topics.hook: **AND: both. OR: either or both. NOT: flip it. XOR: one or the other, not both.**

topics.title: Hardware: the CPU, memory and storage
topics.intro: The CPU is the brain: it fetches, decodes and executes billions of instructions a second. RAM holds what is running now and forgets it when the power goes; storage keeps files safe.
topics.teach: Explain the fetch–decode–execute cycle.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to find out how much RAM and storage the family computer or phone has.
topics.hook: **Fetch, decode, execute**: the CPU’s heartbeat, billions of times a second.

topics.title: Software, operating systems and languages
topics.intro: Software tells the hardware what to do. The operating system manages everything; applications do jobs for us; translators turn the code we write into the machine code the CPU understands.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a compiler and an interpreter.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to name three jobs the operating system does while {she} is using a laptop.
topics.hook: **A compiler translates the whole program first; an interpreter goes line by line.**

topics.title: Networks and the internet
topics.intro: A network connects devices so they can share. The internet is a network of networks; the World Wide Web is just one service that runs on it. Data travels in small packets that can take different routes.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what happens, step by step, when {she} types a website address.
topics.hook: **The internet is the roads; the web is just one kind of traffic on them.**

topics.title: Cybersecurity and staying safe
topics.intro: Criminals attack people as much as computers: phishing emails, guessed passwords and malware. Strong passwords, two-factor authentication, encryption and a healthy suspicion keep data safe.
topics.teach: Explain how to spot a phishing email.
topics.talk: Check together that {her} important accounts use strong, different passwords and two-factor authentication.
topics.hook: **Think before you click**: urgency, odd links and requests for passwords are red flags.

topics.title: The story of computing
topics.intro: From an ancient Greek bronze gearbox that predicted eclipses, to Babbage, Lovelace and Turing, to the phone in your pocket: computing has a surprisingly long history.
topics.teach: Explain why Ada Lovelace is sometimes called the first computer programmer.
topics.talk: Look up a photo of the Antikythera mechanism together.
topics.hook: **Antikythera, Babbage, Lovelace, Turing, Berners-Lee**: gears, engines, code, codebreaking, the web.

topics.title: Computing, ethics and the law
topics.intro: Computers raise big questions: who owns your data, is it fair when an algorithm decides, and what happens to old phones? UK law protects data, punishes hacking and covers copying.
topics.teach: Explain one way an AI system could be unfair, and how to make it fairer.
topics.talk: Discuss with {him}: should a computer ever decide who gets a job interview?
topics.hook: Three UK laws: **Data Protection** (your data), **Computer Misuse** (hacking), **Copyright** (copying).

topics.title: Trace tables
topics.intro: A trace table follows a program line by line, writing down every variable as it changes. It is how GCSE students (and professional programmers) find out exactly what code does.
topics.teach: Explain how to fill in a trace table for a loop.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to trace a Fibonacci loop on paper.
topics.hook: **One column per variable, one new value each time it changes.**

topics.title: Negative numbers in binary
topics.intro: How can 0s and 1s show −5? In two’s complement, the leftmost bit is worth a negative amount (−128 in a byte). It makes subtraction just a kind of addition.
topics.teach: Explain how to turn −20 into 8-bit two’s complement.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what the smallest number in 8-bit two’s complement is.
topics.hook: **Flip the bits and add 1** to make a number negative in two’s complement.

topics.title: Databases and SQL
topics.intro: Databases store huge amounts of data in tables of records and fields. SQL is the language for asking questions of them: SELECT these fields FROM this table WHERE this is true.
topics.teach: Explain what a primary key is and why every table needs one.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to design a table of the Olympian gods: what fields would it need?
topics.hook: **SELECT the fields, FROM the table, WHERE the condition is true.**

topics.title: Network topologies and protocols
topics.intro: Networks can be wired as a star, a mesh or a bus, each with strengths and weaknesses. Protocols are agreed rules, organised in layers, so devices from any maker can talk to each other.
topics.teach: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a star network.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to draw the home network: is it a star?
topics.hook: Star: one hub. Mesh: many routes. TCP/IP layers, top down: **All Teachers Inspire Learners** (Application, Transport, Internet, Link).

items.prompt: Breaking a big problem into smaller, more manageable parts is called…
items.explain: Decomposition: Daedalus planning the labyrinth as walls, corridors and traps, one part at a time.
items.hook: **De-compose = take apart**: split one big problem into smaller ones.
items.example: Planning a party: guests, food, music and games, each sorted out on its own.

items.prompt: Removing unnecessary detail so you can focus on what matters is called…
items.explain: A London Underground map is a famous abstraction: it ignores real distances and shows only the stops and connections.
items.hook: **Abstraction = leave out what doesn’t matter**, like a map that ignores every tree.
items.example: A football formation diagram shows only where the players stand, not their faces or the weather.

items.prompt: Spotting things that problems have in common, so one solution can be reused, is called…
items.explain: Once you can sort one list, the same pattern sorts any list.
items.hook: **Seen it before?** Reuse the solution: that is pattern recognition.
items.example: Once you can follow a recipe for one cake, the same pattern works for muffins and brownies.

items.prompt: What is an algorithm?
items.answer: a precise sequence of steps to solve a problem
distractors: a computer program written in a language like Python
items.explain: An algorithm can be written in English, pseudocode or a flowchart. A program is an algorithm written in a programming language.
items.hook: **An algorithm is a recipe**: precise steps, in order, that anyone could follow.
items.example: A recipe, a flat-pack furniture leaflet and a sat nav’s directions are all algorithms.

items.prompt: Mira draws a map of Odysseus’s voyage showing only the islands and the order he visited them, not the real distances or coastlines. Which technique is she using?

options.text: Abstraction
Decomposition
options.feedback: Decomposition splits a problem into parts. Leaving out detail is abstraction.

options.text: Iteration
options.feedback: Iteration means repeating.

items.explain: Leaving out details that don’t matter for the job is abstraction.
items.hook: Abstraction **removes** detail; decomposition **divides** the problem.
items.example: A bus timetable leaves out the roads and traffic and keeps just the stops and the times.

items.prompt: Which instruction is too vague to be part of an algorithm?

options.text: “Walk until you are near the temple.”
“Walk 200 steps north, then stop at the gate.”
options.feedback: This is precise: a number and a direction.

options.text: “If the gate is locked, turn left.”
options.feedback: This is a precise decision.

items.explain: Algorithms must be unambiguous: “near” means different things to different people. A computer cannot guess.
items.hook: **Computers can’t guess**: every step needs exact numbers or conditions.
items.example: “Bake until golden” works for a person; a smart oven needs “bake at 180 °C for 25 minutes”.

items.prompt: Theo is writing a quiz game about the Greek gods. Which list is the best decomposition?

options.text: Store questions; ask one; check the answer; keep score; show the result
Write the whole game in one go, then test it at the end
options.feedback: That is the opposite of decomposition.

options.text: Design the title screen; pick colours; choose fonts; add sound effects
options.feedback: That is only one small part, and not the most important.

items.explain: Each smaller part can be designed, written and tested on its own.
items.hook: **Small parts, each tested on its own**, then joined together.
items.example: Car factories build engines, seats and doors separately, then put them together.

items.prompt: Put the stages of solving a problem with a computer in a sensible order.
items.explain: Programmers who start typing before they understand the problem usually have to start again.
items.hook: **Understand, design, code, test**: think before you type.
items.example: Builders don’t start laying bricks before the architect has drawn the plans.

items.prompt: In a flowchart, which shape shows a decision (a question with Yes/No answers)?
items.explain: Diamond = decision. It has one way in and two ways out.
items.hook: **Diamond = decision**: its corners point to the different ways out.
items.example: In a getting-ready flowchart, “Is it raining?” is a diamond: yes leads to the umbrella, no to the sunglasses.

items.prompt: In a flowchart, which shape is used for input and output (like “Ask for a name”)?
items.explain: Parallelogram = input or output.
items.hook: **Parallelogram = put in or print out**: the slanted box for input and output.
items.example: A cash machine asking for your PIN and then showing your balance: both are parallelograms.

items.prompt: In a flowchart, which shape shows a process (like “add 1 to score”)?
items.explain: Rectangle = process.
items.hook: **Rectangle = do something**: a process step.
items.example: “Add 1 to score” in a game, or “add the eggs” in a recipe, is a process box.

items.prompt: In a flowchart, which shape is used for Start and Stop?
items.explain: The terminator shape marks where the algorithm begins and ends.
items.hook: **Oval = the ends**: every flowchart starts and stops in a rounded box.

items.prompt: Every algorithm is built from three constructs: sequence, selection and…
items.explain: Sequence (one step after another), selection (decisions) and iteration (repetition).
items.hook: **Sequence, Selection, Iteration**: steps in order, decisions, repeats.
items.example: Brushing teeth: steps in order (sequence), if the tube is empty get more (selection), brush each tooth (iteration).

items.prompt: What is pseudocode?
items.answer: structured English used to plan an algorithm
distractors: a program that compiles but has a hidden bug in it
a programming language designed for beginners
the low-level code that a compiler makes from Python
items.explain: Pseudocode lets you plan the logic without worrying about the exact rules of one language.
items.hook: **Pseudo means pretend**: pseudocode is pretend code, plain English with structure.
items.example: “IF the dough is sticky THEN add flour” is pseudocode for the kitchen.

items.prompt: In a flowchart, an arrow goes from a decision back UP to an earlier box. What does this show?

options.text: Iteration: a loop
Selection with no loop
options.feedback: Going back to an earlier step makes the algorithm repeat.

options.text: An error in the flowchart
options.feedback: It is a normal way to draw a loop.

items.explain: An arrow looping back means those steps repeat until the decision sends the flow onwards.
items.hook: **An arrow going back up = a loop.**
items.example: Shampoo bottles once said “lather, rinse, repeat”: a loop with no condition to stop it!

items.prompt:
This pseudocode runs with heads = 9:
```
IF heads > 7 THEN
    OUTPUT "Hydra!"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Just a snake"
ENDIF
```
What is output?

options.text: Hydra!
Just a snake
options.feedback: 9 > 7 is true, so the THEN part runs.

options.text: Both lines
options.feedback: Only one branch of an IF runs.

items.explain: 9 is greater than 7, so the first branch runs.
items.hook: **Only one branch of an IF runs**: check the condition, then follow that branch alone.
**= stores, == compares**; / gives a float, // drops the remainder, % gives the remainder.
items.example: 17 sweets shared between 5 friends: 17 // 5 = 3 each, and 17 % 5 = 2 left over.

items.prompt: In Python, what data type is "Athena"?
items.explain: Text in quotation marks is a string (str).
items.hook: **Quotation marks mean string**: anything inside them is text, even digits.
items.example: Phone numbers are stored as strings: you never do maths with them, and the leading 0 must stay.

items.prompt: What data type is 3.14 in Python?
items.explain: A float is a number with a decimal point.
items.hook: **Float: the decimal point floats**, so it holds numbers with a fractional part.
items.example: Prices like 2.99 and body temperatures like 36.6 are floats.

items.prompt: A data type that can only be True or False is called…
items.explain: Named after George Boole, a 19th-century mathematician. In Python: bool.
items.hook: **Boolean = two choices only**: True or False, named after George Boole.
items.example: A light switch, a dark-mode setting or a ticked checkbox is a Boolean.

items.prompt:
Kit runs this program and types 5:
```
n = input("How many heads? ")
print(n * 2)
```
What is printed?

options.feedback: input() always gives a string. "5" * 2 repeats it: 55.

options.text: An error
options.feedback: Multiplying a string by a whole number is allowed: it repeats the string.

items.explain: input() always returns a string. To do maths, convert it: int(input(...)).
items.hook: **input() always gives a string**; wrap it in int() before doing maths.
items.example: A web form treats your age as text until the program converts it into a number.

items.prompt: What is the difference between = and == in Python?

options.text: = stores a value in a variable; == compares two values
They are the same, but == is used inside if statements
options.feedback: x = 5 sets x; x == 5 asks “is x 5?”

options.text: == stores a value in a variable; = compares two values
options.feedback: It is the other way round.

items.explain: One equals assigns; two equals compares and gives True or False.
items.hook: **One = sets it; two == checks it.**
items.example: Setting your alarm for 7:00 is =; the phone checking “is it 7:00 yet?” is ==.

items.prompt: In Python 3, what does 7 / 2 give?

options.feedback: 7 // 2 gives 3. A single / always gives a float.
7 % 2 gives the remainder, 1.

items.explain: / is true division, // is whole-number (floor) division, % is the remainder.
items.hook: **/ gives a decimal, // gives whole parts, % gives the leftovers.**
items.example: 7 campers and 2 tents: 7 / 2 = 3.5, but 7 // 2 = 3 per tent with 7 % 2 = 1 camper left over.

items.prompt: Which is NOT a valid Python variable name?

options.text: 2heroes
hero_2
options.feedback: Underscores and digits are fine, as long as the name doesn’t start with a digit.

options.text: heroCount
options.feedback: This is valid.

items.explain: Variable names cannot start with a digit or contain spaces.
items.hook: **Names start with a letter or an underscore**, never a digit, and contain no spaces.

items.prompt: In Python, which symbol starts a comment (a note the computer ignores)?
items.explain: Comments explain code to humans: # this line works out the score.
items.hook: **# starts a note for humans**; Python ignores the rest of the line.
items.example: Comments are like sticky notes in a recipe book: “use less salt next time”.

items.prompt: Which line correctly asks for a number and stores it as an integer?

options.text: age = int(input("Age? "))
age = input(int("Age? "))
options.feedback: int() must go around the input, converting the answer.

options.text: age = int("Age? ")
options.feedback: This tries to convert the question text itself, which fails.

items.explain: input() gets text; int() converts that text to a whole number.
items.hook: **int(input()): convert the answer, not the question.**
**The first True branch wins**; elif and else are only reached if everything above was False.
items.example: A ticket machine: if age < 12, child price; elif age >= 65, senior price; else adult price.

items.prompt: Which Python operator means “is not equal to”?
items.explain: a != b is True when a and b are different.
items.hook: **!= means not equal**: the ! says “not”.
items.example: A login check: if the typed password != the saved password, refuse entry.

items.prompt: How does Python know which lines belong inside an if statement?

options.text: They are indented (usually 4 spaces)
They are inside curly brackets { }, as in JavaScript
options.feedback: Many languages use { }, but Python uses indentation.

options.text: They end with a semicolon
options.feedback: Python does not need semicolons.

items.explain: Indentation is part of Python’s grammar: get it wrong and you get an error, or a logic error.
items.hook: **Indentation is Python’s brackets**: indented lines belong to the line above that ends with a colon.
items.example: Like notes with sub-points: the indented lines belong to the heading above them.

items.prompt: Why use elif instead of a second if?

options.text: elif is only checked if the earlier conditions were False
elif runs faster because it skips the condition check
options.feedback: The point is the logic: only one branch of an if/elif/else chain runs.

options.text: There is no difference; elif is just shorter to type
options.feedback: Two separate ifs can BOTH run; an elif cannot run if the if before it did.

items.explain: In an if/elif/else chain, exactly one branch runs: the first whose condition is True.
items.hook: **elif = else if**: only checked when everything above it was False.
items.example: A grade calculator: if score >= 70, A; elif score >= 60, B. A score of 75 gets only an A.

items.prompt: What is True and False?

options.text: False
True
options.feedback: and needs BOTH sides to be True.

options.text: An error
options.feedback: and works on any two Booleans.

items.explain: and is True only if both are True; or is True if at least one is.
items.hook: **and needs both to be True**: True and False is False.
items.example: You can ride the rollercoaster only if you are tall enough AND have a ticket: one is not enough.

items.prompt:
Ages 13 and over can enter the Hall of Heroes:
```
if age > 13:
    print("Enter")
```
A 13-year-old is refused. What should the condition be?

options.text: age >= 13
age < 13
options.feedback: That would let in only those under 13.

options.text: age == 13
options.feedback: That would refuse everyone over 13.

items.explain: This is a classic boundary error: > leaves out 13 itself, >= includes it.
items.hook: **> leaves out the boundary; >= includes it.**
items.example: A film rated 12 needs age >= 12, so a 12-year-old gets in.

items.hook: **range(start, stop, step) stops before stop**: range(2, 10, 3) gives 2, 5, 8.
items.example: A microwave counting down 30 seconds is a count-controlled loop; a kettle heating until it boils is condition-controlled.

items.prompt: Which numbers does range(5) produce?
items.explain: range(n) starts at 0 and stops BEFORE n, so it gives n values.
items.hook: **range(n) starts at 0 and stops before n**: n numbers in total.
items.example: A list of 5 songs has positions 0 to 4: exactly range(5).

items.prompt: Which loop is condition-controlled?

options.text: while
for i in range(10)
options.feedback: A for loop over range repeats a fixed number of times: count-controlled.

options.text: if
options.feedback: if is selection, not a loop.

items.explain: while keeps going as long as its condition is True.
items.hook: **while = keep going while the condition is True**: condition-controlled.
items.example: A kettle keeps heating while the water is below boiling point.

items.prompt:
What is wrong with this program?
```
lives = 3
while lives > 0:
    print("Fight on!")
```

options.text: lives never changes, so the loop never ends
The while line is missing a colon at the end
options.feedback: The colon is there.

options.text: print cannot be used inside a while loop
options.feedback: print works fine in a loop; the problem is that lives never changes.

items.explain: An infinite loop. The loop body needs lives = lives - 1 (or another way to make the condition False).
items.hook: **Change the condition inside the loop**, or it runs for ever.
items.example: An app stuck on a spinning loading circle may be trapped in a loop that never ends.

items.prompt: Theo wants to keep asking for the password until it is right. Which loop fits best?

options.text: a while loop
a for loop with range(3)
options.feedback: That asks exactly 3 times, even if the password was right first time, or still wrong.

options.text: no loop
options.feedback: He needs to repeat the question.

items.explain: When you don’t know in advance how many repeats you need, use a condition-controlled while loop.
items.hook: **Don’t know how many repeats? Use while.**
items.example: A cash machine keeps asking for your PIN until it is right, or until it locks you out.

items.prompt: What does the keyword break do inside a loop?

options.text: Stops the loop immediately
Skips to the next item
options.feedback: That is continue.

options.text: Crashes the program on purpose
options.feedback: break exits the loop neatly and carries on after it.

items.explain: break jumps straight out of the loop.
items.hook: **break is the emergency exit**: jump straight out of the loop.
items.example: A search can break out as soon as it finds the item, instead of checking the rest.

items.hook: **A list starts counting at 0**, and a slice [1:4] stops just before index 4.
items.example: A playlist is a list: song 0 plays first, and the last song is at index len − 1.

items.prompt: In the list muses = ["Clio", "Calliope", "Urania"], what is muses[0]?

options.text: "Clio"
"Calliope"
options.feedback: Python counts from 0, so index 1 is the second item.

options.text: An error
options.feedback: Index 0 is the first item.

items.explain: Lists are zero-indexed: the first item is at index 0.
items.hook: **A list starts counting at 0**: muses[0] is the first item.
items.example: Like a UK lift: the ground floor is 0, so the first floor up is 1.

items.prompt: muses = ["Clio", "Calliope", "Urania"]. What happens with print(muses[3])?

options.text: IndexError: there is no item at index 3
It prints "Urania", the last item in the list
options.feedback: Urania is at index 2. Three items have indexes 0, 1, 2.

options.text: It prints None because index 3 is empty
options.feedback: Python raises an error.

items.explain: A list of 3 items has indexes 0 to 2. Asking for index 3 is a runtime error.
items.hook: **Last index = length − 1**: 3 items have indexes 0, 1 and 2.
items.example: A three-storey UK house has floors 0, 1 and 2: there is no floor 3.

items.explain: Parameters are the inputs a function expects. The value you pass in when calling it is the argument.

items.prompt: What is the difference between return and print inside a function?

items.prompt: What does len("MEDUSA") give?

items.prompt:

items.explain: Syntax errors break the rules of the language: missing brackets, colons or quotes.
items.hook: **Syntax = grammar**: break the language’s rules and nothing runs at all.
items.example: Like a sentence with a missing bracket or full stop: the reader can’t make sense of it.

items.prompt:
This should find the average of two scores, but gives the wrong answer. What kind of error?

print(average)

items.explain: Runtime errors happen while the program is running, often because of unexpected values.

items.example: An app that crashes when you open a photo it can’t read has hit a runtime error.

items.prompt: A program accepts ages 11 to 18. Testing it with 11 and 18 is called using … test data.
items.explain: Boundary data sits on the edges of the valid range, where mistakes like > instead of >= hide.
items.hook: **Normal, boundary, erroneous**: test inside the range, on its edges, and outside it.
items.example: For a club for ages 11 to 18: test 14 (normal), 11 and 18 (boundary) and banana (erroneous).

items.prompt: Typing “banana” into a program that expects an age is … test data.
items.explain: Erroneous (invalid) data should be rejected politely, not crash the program.
items.hook: **Erroneous = full of error**: data that should be rejected, politely.
items.example: Typing letters into the card-number box on a shopping site should give a polite message, not a crash.

items.prompt: What is a “dry run”?

options.text: Working through code by hand, line by line
Running a program with no input data
options.feedback: It is done on paper, often with a trace table.

options.text: Running a program once before it is finished
options.feedback: A dry run uses no computer at all: you trace the code by hand.

items.explain: Dry runs find logic errors that the computer can’t point out for you.
items.hook: **Dry run = no computer, just pencil and paper.**
items.example: A fire drill is a dry run: practising the steps without a real fire.

items.prompt: Which story made “debugging” a famous word for fixing errors?

options.text: From a famous story of a moth stuck in an early computer
Early programmers were nicknamed “bugs” by engineers
options.feedback: Engineers already called faults “bugs”; a moth found in a computer in 1947 made the word famous.

options.text: Errors look like tiny insects when printed out on paper
options.feedback: The word “bug” for a fault is older, but the moth story made it famous.

items.explain: Operators of the Harvard Mark II found a moth in it in 1947, and Grace Hopper loved telling the story. Engineers had called faults “bugs” before, but the logbook made it famous.
items.hook: **Debugging = removing the bug**: a real moth, taped into a logbook in 1947.
items.example: The logbook page with the moth is kept at the Smithsonian’s history museum in Washington.

items.hook: **Binary search: look in the middle, throw half away**, and repeat.
items.example: Finding a word in a paper dictionary: open it in the middle, decide which half, and keep halving.

items.prompt: What does a binary search need before it can start?

options.text: The data must be sorted
The data must be in binary
options.feedback: “Binary” refers to splitting in two, not to 0s and 1s.

options.text: The data must be numbers
options.feedback: It works on sorted words too.

items.explain: Binary search compares with the middle and throws away half. That only makes sense if the list is in order.
items.hook: **No order, no binary search**: halving only works when you know which half to keep.
items.example: You can halve your way through a dictionary because it is alphabetical; a shuffled pile of papers needs a linear search.

items.prompt: When is a linear search a better choice than a binary search?

options.text: When the list is small or not sorted
When the list is huge and already sorted
options.feedback: That is exactly when binary search shines.

options.text: Never
options.feedback: Linear search works on unsorted lists, and is simple for small ones.

items.explain: Sorting a list just to search it once can take longer than a linear search.
items.hook: **Small or unsorted? Go linear.**
items.example: Looking for your keys in a small bag, you just check everything.

items.prompt: About how many checks does a binary search need, at most, to find an item among a million sorted items?
items.explain: 2^{20} is just over a million, and each check halves the list.
items.hook: **2¹⁰ ≈ 1000, so 2²⁰ ≈ a million**: 20 halvings.
items.example: “Guess my number” from 1 to a million takes at most 20 guesses if you always halve.

items.prompt: In the WORST case, how many items does a linear search check in a list of n items?

options.text: n: every item
1: only the first item
options.feedback: That is the best case (found first time).

options.text: n ÷ 2: half the items
options.feedback: That is roughly the average, not the worst.

items.explain: The worst case is when the item is last, or not there at all.
items.hook: **Worst case = check them all.**
items.example: Hunting for one picture in an unsorted photo album might mean turning every page.

items.hook: **Bubble sort: the biggest value bubbles to the end** on every pass.
items.example: Sorting playing cards one at a time into your hand is insertion sort; combining two sorted piles is a merge.

items.prompt: How does a bubble sort know the list is sorted?

options.text: A whole pass happens with no swaps
It counts the items
options.feedback: It needs to check the order, not the number of items.

options.text: After exactly one pass through the whole list
options.feedback: One pass only guarantees the largest item is at the end.

items.explain: If no neighbours needed swapping, everything is in order.
items.hook: **A whole pass with no swaps means it is sorted.**

items.prompt: Merge sort is an example of which strategy?

options.text: Divide and conquer
Brute force
options.feedback: Brute force tries every possibility.

options.text: Trial and improvement
options.feedback: Merge sort is a precise algorithm.

items.explain: It splits the list into halves until each piece has one item, then merges the pieces in order.
items.hook: **Merge sort = divide and conquer**: split, split, split, then merge.
items.example: Two teachers each sort half the exam papers, then merge their piles: quicker than one sorting them all.

items.prompt: Which is usually fastest for sorting a very large list?

options.text: Merge sort
Bubble sort
options.feedback: Bubble sort is simple but very slow on large lists.

options.text: Insertion sort
options.feedback: Insertion sort is good for small or nearly sorted lists, slow for huge ones.

items.explain: For a million items, bubble sort could need around half a trillion comparisons; merge sort needs about 20 million.
items.hook: **Bubble sort crawls on big lists; merge sort scales.**
items.example: Online shops sorting millions of products by price rely on fast methods like merge sort.

items.prompt: Which everyday activity is most like an insertion sort?

options.text: Picking up cards one at a time and sliding each into place
Splitting a pile of cards in half again and again
options.feedback: That is more like merge sort.

options.text: Swapping neighbouring books on a shelf until none are out of order
options.feedback: That is bubble sort.

items.explain: Insertion sort grows a sorted section one item at a time.
items.hook: **Insertion sort = sorting a hand of cards.**
items.example: Adding a new pupil to an alphabetical register: slide the name into the right place.

items.hook: **Binary place values double**: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Add up the columns with a 1.
items.example: Each colour channel of a phone photo uses 8 bits, so it has 256 levels, from 0 to 255.

items.hook: **One hex digit = 4 bits**: split the binary into nibbles; A = 10, B = 11 … F = 15.
items.example: Web colours are hex: #FF8800 is full red, about half green and no blue, which makes orange.

items.prompt: Why do computers use binary?

options.text: Their transistors are switches: either on or off
Binary is easier for humans to read and check
options.feedback: Humans find binary hard. That’s why we use hex!

options.text: It uses less electricity than storing denary digits
options.feedback: The reason is that switches have two states.

items.explain: Two states (on/off, 1/0) are easy to build reliably with billions of tiny switches.
items.hook: **Two states: on/off, 1/0**. A transistor is just a tiny switch.
items.example: A light switch is the simplest bit: off is 0, on is 1.

items.prompt: How many bits are in a byte?
items.explain: A byte is 8 bits; half a byte (4 bits) is a nibble.
items.hook: **A byte bites 8 bits.**
items.example: One byte stores one letter of plain English text, so HELLO takes 5 bytes.

items.prompt: What is 4 bits called?
items.explain: A nibble is half a byte, and it matches exactly one hexadecimal digit.
items.hook: **A nibble is a small bite**: half a byte, 4 bits, exactly one hex digit.

items.prompt: Why do programmers often use hexadecimal?

options.text: It is shorter than binary and converts to it easily
Computers store all their data in hexadecimal
options.feedback: Computers store binary. Hex is only for humans.

options.text: Hex numbers take up less memory than binary ones
options.feedback: It makes no difference to memory.

items.explain: One hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so FF is far easier to read and type than 11111111.
items.hook: **Hex is shorthand**: one hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits.
items.example: Network MAC addresses are written in hex: 12 hex digits instead of 48 binary digits.

items.prompt: On the web, the colour #FF0000 means full red, no green, no blue. What is FF in denary?

options.feedback: F is 15, but FF is 15 × 16 + 15.
FF = 255, the biggest value one byte can hold.

items.explain: Each pair of hex digits is one byte: 0 to 255 for red, green and blue.
items.hook: **FF = 15 × 16 + 15 = 255**, the biggest value one byte can hold.
items.example: On any web page, #FFFFFF is white (every colour full on) and #000000 is black.

items.hook: **0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 1 = 10, 1 + 1 + 1 = 11**: write the right digit, carry the left one.
items.example: An 8-bit counter at 255 that adds 1 overflows to 0, like a car’s mileometer rolling over to zeros.

items.hook: **Shift left = × 2 per place; shift right = ÷ 2 per place**, just as moving digits in denary is × or ÷ 10.
items.example: Shifting 00000101 (5) two places left gives 00010100 (20): four times as big.

items.prompt: In binary, what is 1 + 1?
items.explain: 1 + 1 = 2, and 2 in binary is 10: write 0, carry 1.
items.hook: **There is no digit 2 in binary**: 1 + 1 = 10, write 0, carry 1.
items.example: Like a mileometer: when a wheel passes its last digit it goes back to 0 and nudges the next wheel on.

items.prompt: In binary, what is 1 + 1 + 1?
items.explain: 3 in binary is 11: write 1, carry 1.

items.prompt: What is an overflow error?

options.text: A result too big to fit in the bits available
Too many programs are open at once for the RAM
options.feedback: That is about memory, not overflow.

options.text: A number with more digits than the screen can show
options.feedback: Not this kind of overflow!

items.explain: With 8 bits, anything over 255 overflows: the extra carry is lost.
items.hook: **Too big for the bits = overflow**: 8 bits stop at 255.
items.example: The Year 2000 bug came from storing years with only two digits, so 2000 looked like 1900: not enough room.

items.prompt: What does a right shift of 1 place do to a binary number?

options.text: Halves it (dropping any remainder)
Doubles it (adding a 0 on the right)

options.text: Makes it negative (flipping the first bit)

**A = 65, a = 97**: each lowercase letter is exactly 32 more than its capital.

items.example: A 64 GB phone holds 64 000 MB: room for about 16 000 photos of 4 MB each.

items.hook: **Image = width × height × colour depth**; sound = sample rate × bit depth × seconds. Then ÷ 8 for bytes.
items.example: A 12-megapixel photo at 24 bits per pixel is 36 MB before compression, which is why phones save JPEGs.

items.prompt: Why was Unicode invented when ASCII already existed?

options.text: ASCII’s 128 characters were not enough for every language
ASCII was too slow for sending text over the internet
options.feedback: The problem was the number of characters.

options.text: ASCII could not store capital letters or punctuation
options.feedback: It can: A is 65.

items.explain: Unicode can represent over a million characters, including α β γ and emoji.
items.hook: **ASCII: 128 characters. Unicode: room for over a million**, enough for every alphabet and emoji.
items.example: An emoji in a text is a Unicode character, so any phone knows which emoji it is, though each maker draws it a little differently.

items.prompt: The smallest single dot of colour in a digital image is called a…
items.explain: Short for “picture element”.
items.hook: **Pixel = picture element**: the tiny coloured squares that make up an image.
items.example: Zoom right in on a phone photo and you will see the separate coloured squares: pixels.

items.prompt: The number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel is called the…
items.explain: More bits per pixel mean more possible colours: 24-bit colour gives over 16 million.
items.hook: **Colour depth of n bits → 2ⁿ colours**: 24 bits give over 16 million.
items.example: A GIF can hold at most 256 colours (8 bits), which is why GIF photos can look blotchy.

items.prompt: The number of pixels in an image (for example 1920 × 1080) is its…
items.explain: Higher resolution means more detail and a bigger file.
items.hook: **Resolution = how many pixels**: width × height.
items.example: Full HD is 1920 × 1080, about 2 million pixels; 4K has four times as many.

items.prompt: The number of times per second a sound is measured when it is recorded is the…
items.explain: CD audio uses 44,100 samples per second.
items.hook: **Sample rate = snapshots per second** of the sound wave.
items.example: CD audio takes 44 100 samples a second, more than twice the highest pitch people can hear.

items.prompt: Which kind of compression permanently removes some data to make a file smaller?

options.text: Lossy compression
Lossless compression
options.feedback: Lossless can be undone exactly.

options.text: Encryption
options.feedback: Encryption scrambles data; it doesn’t make it smaller.

items.explain: JPEG photos and MP3 music use lossy compression; the removed detail is hard for people to notice.
items.hook: **Lossy loses it for good**: JPEG photos and MP3 music.
items.example: Messaging apps often shrink your photos with lossy compression, so your friend’s copy is lower quality.

items.prompt: Which file needs LOSSLESS compression?

options.text: A Python program
A holiday photo
options.feedback: Tiny changes to a photo are invisible, so lossy is fine.

options.text: A song for a phone
options.feedback: MP3s use lossy compression happily.

items.explain: Losing even one character could break a program, so text and code must be compressed losslessly (like ZIP).
items.hook: **Lossless = nothing lost**: a ZIP file gives back every bit.
items.example: Sending homework as a ZIP file is safe: every character comes back exactly.

items.prompt: Run-length encoding stores AAAAABBB as 5A3B. What is the original of 3Z2E4U?

options.text: ZZZEEUUUU
ZEU
options.feedback: The numbers say how many of each letter.

options.text: 3Z2E4U
options.feedback: That is the compressed version.

items.explain: RLE replaces runs of the same value with a count and the value: a simple lossless method.
items.hook: **RLE = count, then value**: 5A means AAAAA.
items.example: Fax machines used run-length encoding, because a page is mostly long runs of white.

items.prompt: Data stored with a photo about the photo itself (date, camera, location) is called…

options.text: metadata
pixels
options.feedback: Pixels are the picture itself.

options.text: a virus
options.feedback: Metadata is normal, though it can reveal where you were.

items.explain: Metadata is “data about data”. Location metadata on a photo can show where you live, so check it before sharing.
items.hook: **Meta means about**: metadata is data about the data.
items.example: A photo’s metadata can include the exact GPS location where it was taken.

items.hook: **AND is like multiplying, OR is like adding (but never above 1)**: 1 AND 0 = 0, 1 OR 0 = 1.
items.example: A car alarm sounds if (a door opens OR a window breaks) AND the alarm is set.

items.prompt: Which logic gate gives 1 only when BOTH inputs are 1?
items.explain: AND: both must be true.
items.hook: **AND = both**, like needing a ticket AND a passport to board a plane.
items.example: A microwave only runs if the door is shut AND the start button is pressed.

items.prompt: Which logic gate gives 1 when at least one input is 1?
items.explain: OR: either or both.
items.hook: **OR = either, or both.**
items.example: A doorbell that rings when the front OR the back door button is pressed.

items.prompt: Which logic gate has one input and flips it?
items.explain: NOT 1 = 0 and NOT 0 = 1. It is also called an inverter.
items.hook: **NOT flips it**: 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1.
items.example: An automatic night light: light on = NOT daylight.

items.prompt: Which gate gives 1 when exactly one input is 1, but not both?
items.explain: XOR means “exclusive or”. Computers use XOR gates when adding binary numbers.
items.hook: **XOR = exclusive or**: one or the other, but not both.

items.prompt: A lamp in the temple can be switched on from the door OR the altar, but turns off if both switches are on. Which gate is this?

options.text: XOR
OR
options.feedback: OR would stay on when both are on.

options.text: AND
options.feedback: AND would need both on.

items.explain: Exactly one switch on: that is XOR. Landing lights with a switch at each end of the stairs work this way.
items.hook: **Two switches, one light = XOR**: flipping either switch changes the light.
items.example: Long corridors often have a light switch at each end, wired in exactly this way.

items.prompt: In a truth table for A AND B, how many rows give an output of 1?

options.feedback: Only A = 1, B = 1 gives 1.
That would be OR.

items.explain: Of the four rows (00, 01, 10, 11), only 11 gives 1.
items.hook: **n inputs → 2ⁿ rows**; AND has just one 1, in the 1, 1 row.

items.prompt: What are logic gates built from inside a processor?

options.text: Transistors: tiny electronic switches
Tiny light bulbs that switch on and off
options.feedback: Early computers used valves; modern ones use transistors.

options.text: Magnets that store a 1 or a 0
options.feedback: Transistors, billions of them.

items.explain: A modern processor contains billions of transistors, each only tens of nanometres across, about the size of a virus.
items.hook: **Transistors are switches**, and each gate is built from a handful of them.
items.example: A modern phone chip packs over 10 billion transistors into something the size of a fingernail.

items.prompt: Which part of a computer fetches, decodes and executes instructions?
items.explain: The Central Processing Unit is the computer’s brain.
items.hook: **CPU = Central Processing Unit**: the brain that fetches, decodes and executes.
items.example: When a phone gets warm during a game, much of that heat comes from its busy processor.

items.prompt: Put the CPU’s cycle in order.
items.explain: Fetch the instruction from memory, decode what it means, execute it. Then repeat, billions of times a second.
items.hook: **Fetch, decode, execute**: get it, work out what it means, do it.
items.example: Like following a recipe: read the next step, work out what it means, then do it.

items.prompt: Which memory holds the programs and data in use right now, but loses everything when the power goes off?
items.explain: RAM is volatile: it forgets when switched off.
items.hook: **RAM forgets**: it is volatile, like writing on a steamed-up mirror.
items.example: Unsaved homework vanishes in a power cut because it was only in RAM.

items.prompt: Which memory keeps the start-up instructions even when the power is off, and normally cannot be changed?
items.explain: Read-Only Memory is non-volatile. It holds the instructions to boot the computer.
items.hook: **ROM = Read-Only Memory**: it remembers the start-up steps even when the power is off.
items.example: When you switch on a laptop, the first instructions it runs come from ROM.

items.prompt: A small amount of very fast memory inside or next to the CPU, holding instructions it uses often, is called…
items.explain: Cache is much faster than RAM, but much smaller and more expensive.
items.hook: **Cache = the pencil case on your desk**: what you use most, close at hand.
items.example: Web browsers keep a cache too: pictures from sites you visit load faster the next time.

items.prompt: Clock speed is measured in gigahertz. What does 3 GHz mean?
items.explain: Giga means a billion. Each tick of the clock is a chance to carry out an instruction.
items.hook: **Giga = billion**: 3 GHz is 3 billion ticks a second.
items.example: A typical laptop processor runs at about 2 to 4 GHz.

items.prompt: What is the main benefit of a quad-core processor?

options.text: It can process up to four tasks at once

items.explain: Each core is like a separate processor, but software must be written to use them all.

items.prompt: Why do most laptops now use an SSD instead of a hard disk drive?

options.text: It has no moving parts, so it is faster and tougher

items.explain: SSDs use flash memory; hard disks have spinning magnetic platters and a moving read/write head.

items.example: A laptop with an SSD is less likely to lose files if it is dropped than one with a spinning hard disk.

items.prompt: Which type of storage uses spinning magnetic platters?

options.text: A hard disk drive (HDD)
A solid-state drive (SSD)

options.text: A Blu-ray disc

items.explain: Magnetic (HDD), solid-state (SSD, USB sticks), optical (CD, DVD, Blu-ray).

items.prompt: A washing machine has a tiny computer that does just one job. This is called…

a supercomputer
options.feedback: Supercomputers are huge general-purpose machines.

options.text: a server
options.feedback: A server provides services to other computers.

items.explain: Embedded systems are everywhere: cars, microwaves, traffic lights, fitness watches.

items.example: Traffic lights, smart doorbells and car engines all contain embedded systems.

items.prompt: In the von Neumann architecture used by most computers, where are programs stored?
