items.prompt: Windows, macOS, Android and Linux are all examples of…
items.explain: The operating system manages the hardware and runs all the other software.
items.hook: **The OS is the manager**: it runs the hardware and every other program.
items.example: Phones run Android or iOS; laptops often run Windows, macOS or Linux.

items.prompt: Which of these is a job of the operating system?

options.text: Managing memory and sharing the CPU
Writing and checking your essays
options.feedback: That is application software, like a word processor.

options.text: Designing websites and editing photos
options.feedback: That is done with applications.

items.explain: OS jobs: memory management, multitasking, file management, the user interface, drivers for hardware, and security.
items.hook: **OS jobs: memory, multitasking, files, users, devices and security.**

items.prompt: Antivirus, backup and disk defragmentation programs are examples of … software.
items.explain: Utility software helps keep the computer running well.
items.hook: **Utilities are the computer’s maintenance crew.**
items.example: An antivirus scan, or an automatic backup each night, is utility software at work.

items.prompt: What is a high-level language?

options.text: A language like Python that must be translated for the CPU
The machine code the CPU runs directly, with no translation
options.feedback: That is the lowest level.

options.text: A language only for advanced programmers
options.feedback: High-level means far from the hardware, not difficult.

items.explain: High-level languages are easy for people; low-level languages (assembly, machine code) are close to the hardware.
items.hook: **High-level = close to human language; low-level = close to the hardware.**
items.example: Python reads almost like English: print(score) is far easier to read than machine code.

items.prompt: What does a compiler do?

options.text: Translates the whole program before it runs
Translates and runs the program one line at a time
options.feedback: That is an interpreter.

options.text: Checks the program for viruses before it runs
options.feedback: That is antivirus software.

items.explain: Compiled programs run fast and can be shared without the source code; interpreters are handy while developing.
items.hook: **Compiler = translate the whole book first; interpreter = a live translator, sentence by sentence.**
items.example: Big games are usually compiled, so they run fast on your device.

items.prompt: Python is usually run by an interpreter. What does that mean?

options.text: Each line is translated and run in turn
The whole program is translated before any of it runs
options.feedback: That is a compiler.

options.text: It is translated into another human language
options.feedback: It is translated into instructions the CPU can carry out.

items.explain: That’s why a Python program can run its first part and then stop with a runtime error on a later line.
items.hook: **Interpreter = line by line**, so it stops at the first line with an error.
items.example: A live interpreter at a conference translates each sentence as it is spoken.

items.prompt: What is open-source software?

options.text: Software whose code anyone can read, change and share
Software that is checked to be free of bugs
options.feedback: Open source can still have bugs, but anyone can fix them.

options.text: Software that can only be used online, in a browser
options.feedback: It is about the source code being open.

items.explain: Linux, Firefox and Python itself are open source. Proprietary software keeps its code secret.
items.hook: **Open source = an open recipe**: anyone can read, change and share the code.
items.example: Thousands of volunteers around the world help improve open-source projects such as Linux and Firefox.

items.prompt: The binary instructions a CPU can carry out directly are called…
items.explain: Every program must end up as machine code before the CPU can run it.
items.hook: **Machine code = 1s and 0s**: the only language the CPU really speaks.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a LAN and a WAN?

options.text: A LAN covers a small area; a WAN covers a large one
A LAN is wireless; a WAN always uses fibre cables
options.feedback: Both can use cables or wireless. The difference is the area.

options.text: A LAN is private; a WAN is open to anyone online
options.feedback: Local Area Network vs Wide Area Network.

items.explain: The internet is the biggest WAN of all.
items.hook: **LAN = Local (one building); WAN = Wide (across a country or the world).**
items.example: Your home Wi-Fi is a LAN; the internet linking it to the rest of the world is a WAN.

items.prompt: What is the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web?

options.text: The internet is the network; the web is pages you visit on it
They are two names for the same worldwide network
options.feedback: Email and online games use the internet but are not the web.

options.text: The web is the cables; the internet is the websites
options.feedback: It is the other way round: the internet is the network, and the web runs on it.

items.explain: The web is one service that runs on the internet, like email or video calls.
items.hook: **The internet is the roads; the web is the shops along them.**
items.example: Email and online gaming use the internet without using the web.

items.prompt: Data sent over the internet is split into small pieces called…
items.explain: Each packet has the destination address and a number, so it can be reassembled in order.
items.hook: **Packets are like numbered postcards**: each has an address and a number, so they can be put back in order.
items.example: A video call is chopped into hundreds of packets a second, and a few lost ones make the picture glitch.

items.prompt: Why can packets from the same email take different routes across the internet?

options.text: Each takes the quickest route at that moment
Because the email is copied to several servers first
options.feedback: Copies are not the reason: each packet is routed separately (packet switching).

options.text: To confuse hackers who might be watching one route
options.feedback: Packets take different routes to avoid busy or broken links.

items.explain: Packet switching makes the internet fast and reliable: if one route fails, packets go another way.
items.hook: **Packet switching: each packet finds its own way**, like cars avoiding a traffic jam.
items.example: If a cable under the sea is cut, packets are simply rerouted another way.

items.prompt: Which system converts a web address like bbc.co.uk into an IP address?
items.explain: The Domain Name System is like the internet’s phone book.
items.hook: **DNS = the internet’s phone book**: names go in, IP addresses come out.
items.example: Before loading a web page, your device looks up the site’s IP address with DNS.

items.prompt: Every device on the internet has a number like 192.168.1.10 that identifies it. What is it called?
items.explain: Internet Protocol address. IPv4 addresses are four numbers from 0 to 255.
items.hook: **An IP address is a postal address** for a device on a network.
items.example: Home routers often give devices addresses beginning 192.168.

items.prompt: What does a router do?

options.text: Forwards packets between different networks
Stores copies of the websites you visit
options.feedback: Servers store websites.

options.text: Makes the internet faster than your plan allows
options.feedback: A router forwards data; it can’t add bandwidth.

items.explain: A switch connects devices within one network; a router connects networks to each other.
items.hook: **A router is a postal sorting office**: it sends each packet towards the right network.
items.example: The box your home Wi-Fi comes from is a router linking your LAN to the internet.

items.prompt: What does the S in HTTPS mean, and why does it matter?

options.text: Secure: the data sent is encrypted
Speedy: pages load faster over the connection
options.feedback: It means secure.

options.text: Simple: an easier version of HTTP
options.feedback: It adds encryption, which is more complex, not simpler.

items.explain: With HTTPS, anyone intercepting the packets sees scrambled data, not your password.
items.hook: **S = Secure**: the data is encrypted on its way, but check the web address too, because scam sites can use HTTPS.
items.example: Online banking and shopping use HTTPS, so card numbers are scrambled on the way.

items.prompt: An agreed set of rules for how data is sent between devices is called a…
items.explain: HTTP, HTTPS, TCP/IP and SMTP (email) are all protocols.
items.hook: **Protocol = agreed rules**, like everyone driving on the left in the UK.
items.example: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and email all follow protocols, so devices from different makers can talk.

items.prompt: The amount of data that can be sent across a connection per second is called…
items.explain: Measured in megabits per second (Mbps).
items.hook: **Bandwidth = the width of the pipe**: wider pipe, more data each second.
items.example: Streaming a 4K film needs far more bandwidth than streaming music.

items.hook: **Shift each letter along the alphabet**; to decode, shift back. After Z, wrap round to A.
items.example: ROT13, a Caesar shift of 13, was once used online to hide puzzle answers: doing it twice gets the text back.

items.prompt: An email pretending to be from your bank, asking you to “confirm your password”, is called…
items.explain: Phishing tricks people into giving away details. Real banks never ask for your password by email.
items.hook: **Phishing = fishing for your details** with bait.
items.example: A text saying your parcel is held and you must pay £1.99 through a link is a common phishing trick.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest clue that an email is a phishing attempt?

options.text: It urges you to log in via a link, from an odd address
It arrives early in the morning while you are asleep
options.feedback: Timing tells you nothing.

options.text: It has the company logo and a polite greeting
options.feedback: Logos are easy to copy. Look at the sender address and the link.

items.explain: Urgency, threats, odd addresses and links that go somewhere unexpected are classic signs.
items.hook: **Urgent + a link + an odd address = red flag.** Check where a link really goes before clicking.
items.example: A message from your bank sent from a random free email address is a classic warning sign.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest password?

options.text: Purple-Hydra-Sails-42!
Athena-Athena-Athena-Athena
options.feedback: Repeating one common word is easy to guess, however long it is.

options.text: P@ssw0rd2024!
options.feedback: Swapping letters for symbols in “Password” is one of the first things crackers try.

items.explain: Long passwords made of random words, with symbols and numbers, are strong and memorable.
items.hook: **Three random words** make a password that is strong and easy to remember.
items.example: The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre recommends three random words, like PurpleHydraSails.

items.prompt: What is two-factor authentication?

options.text: Proving it’s you in two separate ways
Typing your password twice to make sure it is right
options.feedback: That is still just one factor.

options.text: Having two passwords for two different accounts
options.feedback: Both are things you know: still one kind of factor.

items.explain: Even if a criminal steals your password, they still need your phone.
items.hook: **Something you know + something you have** (or something you are).
items.example: A code texted to your phone after you type your password is two-factor authentication.

items.prompt: Malware that locks or encrypts your files and demands payment to unlock them is called…
items.explain: Backups are the best defence: you can restore your files without paying.
items.hook: **Ransomware holds your files to ransom**; backups set you free.
items.example: In 2017 the WannaCry ransomware hit NHS hospitals, and thousands of appointments were cancelled.

items.prompt: Why is a Trojan horse a good name for a type of malware?

options.text: It pretends to be useful but hides something harmful
It spreads by itself across networks like an army
options.feedback: That is a worm.

options.text: It attacks computers by flooding them with traffic
options.feedback: That is a denial-of-service attack. The name comes from the wooden horse that hid soldiers at Troy.

items.explain: Just like the wooden horse, the user welcomes it in.
items.hook: “**Beware of Greeks bearing gifts**”: a Trojan hides harm inside something welcome.
items.example: A free game download that secretly installs spyware is a Trojan.

items.prompt: What makes a worm different from a virus?

options.text: A worm spreads by itself; a virus needs a file opened
Worms are harmless; viruses always delete files
options.feedback: Worms can do serious damage and spread very fast.

options.text: A virus spreads by itself; a worm needs a file opened
options.feedback: It is the other way round.

items.explain: Both are malware (malicious software).
items.hook: **A worm wriggles about by itself**; a virus needs someone to open its host file.
items.example: A worm can spread across a whole company network overnight without anyone clicking anything.

items.prompt: What is encryption?

options.text: Scrambling data so only the key holder can read it
Deleting data safely so nobody can recover it
options.feedback: Encryption keeps data, but makes it unreadable without the key.

options.text: Making a hidden backup copy of the data
options.feedback: Backups copy data; encryption protects it.

items.explain: Julius Caesar used a simple shift cipher; modern encryption uses keys with hundreds of digits.
items.hook: **Encryption = a locked box**: only the key holder can open it.
items.example: Many messaging apps use end-to-end encryption, so even the company running the app can’t read your chats.

items.prompt: Someone phones Kit pretending to be from the school IT team and asks for a password “to fix the account”. This is…

options.text: social engineering
a firewall
options.feedback: A firewall blocks network traffic.

options.text: a software update
options.feedback: It is a trick aimed at the person, not the computer.

items.explain: Social engineering attacks people rather than machines. IT staff never need your password.
items.hook: **Social engineering hacks the human**, not the computer.
items.example: A caller pretending to be from your bank and asking for a code is social engineering.

items.prompt: What does a firewall do?

options.text: Blocks network traffic that isn’t allowed
Stops the computer from overheating under load
options.feedback: It is about network traffic.

options.text: Removes viruses already on the computer
options.feedback: That is antivirus software.

items.explain: Think of it as the guard at the city gate.
items.hook: **A firewall is the guard at the city gate**: it checks what comes in and goes out.
items.example: School networks use firewalls to block unsafe websites and attacks from outside.

items.prompt: Mira posts a photo outside her school, in uniform, with her full name. What is the main risk?

options.text: Strangers could work out where she is every day
The photo might be reused in a school newsletter
options.feedback: The worry is what it reveals.

options.text: No risk, if her account is private
options.feedback: Followers can share or screenshot posts, and accounts can be hacked.

items.explain: Your digital footprint can last for ever. Think before sharing your location, school or routine.
items.hook: **Your digital footprint is a trail** that is very hard to wash away.
items.example: Employers and universities sometimes search applicants’ names online.

items.prompt: What is the Antikythera mechanism?

options.text: An ancient Greek geared device for predicting eclipses
The first electronic computer, built in the 1940s
options.feedback: It is bronze gears, not electronics, but it was an analogue computer.

options.text: A Roman water clock used to time speeches
options.feedback: It was found in a Greek shipwreck and is a calculating device.

items.explain: Found in a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera in 1901, it is often called the oldest known analogue computer.
items.hook: **Antikythera: ancient gears that predicted the sky**, the oldest known analogue computer.
items.example: Divers found it in a shipwreck in 1901; X-ray scans later revealed about 30 surviving gears.

items.prompt: Which Victorian mathematician designed the Analytical Engine, a mechanical general-purpose computer?
items.explain: It was never finished in his lifetime, but its design had memory and a processor, like a modern computer.
items.hook: **Babbage designed the engine; Lovelace wrote its program.**
items.example: In 1991 London’s Science Museum built Babbage’s Difference Engine No. 2 from his plans, and it worked.

items.prompt: Who wrote notes in 1843 including an algorithm for the Analytical Engine, often called the first computer program?
items.explain: She also saw that computers could one day work with music and pictures, not just numbers.
items.hook: **Ada Lovelace, 1843: the first published algorithm** for a computing machine.
items.example: Ada Lovelace Day, each October, celebrates women in science, technology, engineering and maths.

items.prompt: Which mathematician worked at Bletchley Park breaking German codes and is called a father of computer science?
items.explain: He described the “Turing machine” in 1936 and the Turing test for artificial intelligence in 1950.
items.hook: **Turing: Bletchley Park, the Turing machine, the Turing test.**
items.example: Alan Turing’s portrait appears on the Bank of England £50 note.

items.prompt: Colossus (1944) is famous because it was…

options.text: an early electronic computer built to break codes
the first computer ever to connect to the internet
options.feedback: The internet did not exist until decades later; Colossus was a wartime code-breaker.

options.text: a giant calculator used to design the Spitfire
options.feedback: It was a code-breaking computer at Bletchley Park, not a design tool.

items.explain: It was designed by the engineer Tommy Flowers and used about 2,400 valves in its Mark 2 version (the first had about 1,600).
items.hook: **Colossus was colossal**: a room-sized electronic codebreaker.
items.example: A working rebuild of Colossus can be seen at the National Museum of Computing at Bletchley Park.

items.prompt: Why was the invention of the transistor in 1947 so important?

options.text: It replaced big, hot valves, so computers could shrink
It let computers connect to the internet for the first time
options.feedback: The internet came decades later.

options.text: It made computers mechanical, with moving gears
options.feedback: It made them smaller electronic machines.

items.explain: A modern phone chip has billions of transistors.
items.hook: **The transistor replaced the valve**: smaller, cooler, cheaper and more reliable.
items.example: Pocket transistor radios of the 1950s were among the first gadgets the transistor made possible.

items.prompt: Who invented the World Wide Web in 1989?
items.explain: He was working at CERN in Switzerland, and the web was given to the world free.
items.hook: **Tim Berners-Lee, CERN, 1989: the World Wide Web.**
items.example: The first website, made at CERN, can still be visited today.

items.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
items.explain: Computing ideas are very old; electronic computers are less than 100 years old.
items.hook: **Gears, then engines, then valves, then the web**: ancient Greece, the 1830s, 1944, 1989.

items.prompt: Which UK law makes it illegal to hack into a computer without permission?
items.explain: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 covers unauthorised access and spreading malware.
items.hook: **Computer Misuse Act 1990 = the hacking law.**
items.example: Logging into a friend’s account without permission, even as a joke, can break this law.

items.prompt: Which UK law controls how organisations collect, store and use people’s personal data?
items.explain: The Data Protection Act 2018 (with the UK GDPR): data must be kept safe, accurate and only used for its stated purpose.
items.hook: **Data Protection Act = your data, your rights**: kept safe, accurate and no longer than needed.
items.example: You can ask any organisation for a copy of the personal data it holds about you.

items.prompt: Theo downloads a film from an illegal site and shares it with friends. Which law does this break?

options.text: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act
The Computer Misuse Act
options.feedback: He didn’t hack anything; he copied someone else’s work.

options.text: No law, because the film was already online
options.feedback: Copyright law applies online too.

items.explain: Creators own the right to copy and share their work.
items.hook: **Copyright: the right to copy belongs to the creator.**
items.example: Using a song in your video without permission can get the video muted or taken down.

items.prompt: An AI that helps choose job applicants was trained mostly on data about past male employees. What is the risk?

options.text: It may unfairly favour men
None: computers are always fair
options.feedback: Computers learn patterns from data, including unfair ones.

options.text: It will reject everyone who applies
options.feedback: It will work, but unfairly.

items.explain: AI is only as fair as the data it learns from. That’s why people must check its decisions.
items.hook: **Biased data in, biased decisions out.**

items.prompt: What is the biggest environmental problem with throwing away old phones?

options.text: They contain toxic chemicals and metals worth recycling
They take up a lot of space in landfill sites
options.feedback: The real problem is toxic materials and wasted metals.

options.text: There is no problem, because phones are mostly glass
options.feedback: E-waste is one of the fastest-growing kinds of rubbish.

items.explain: Recycling recovers gold, copper and rare metals, and keeps poisons out of landfill.
items.hook: **Reduce, reuse, recycle**, old tech included.
items.example: A tonne of old phones holds far more gold than a tonne of gold ore, so recycling them really pays.

items.prompt: What is the “digital divide”?

options.text: The gap between people with and without good internet access
A kind of division used in binary arithmetic
options.feedback: It is a social issue.

options.text: The split between Apple users and Android users
options.feedback: It means unequal access to technology.

items.explain: It affects school work, job applications and even seeing a doctor.
items.hook: **The digital divide is the gap between the connected and the unconnected.**
items.example: When schools closed in 2020, some pupils had no laptop or internet for online lessons.

items.prompt: Why are “deepfake” videos a problem?

options.text: AI can show people doing things they never did
They are too large to download on most phones
options.feedback: The problem is trust, not file size.

options.text: They are always obviously fake to anyone watching
options.feedback: Many are very convincing.

items.explain: Check the source before believing or sharing a shocking video.
items.hook: **Deepfake = deep learning + fake.**
items.example: Fraudsters have used AI-copied voices to pretend to be family members asking for money.

items.hook: **One column per variable; write a new value every time it changes.**
items.example: Keeping score in a board game, writing each new total under the last, is a trace table in real life.

items.prompt: What is a trace table for?

options.text: Recording each variable’s value as a program runs
Drawing a flowchart of the program’s structure
options.feedback: Flowcharts show the design; trace tables follow it running.

options.text: Storing the program’s results in a table
options.feedback: That is a database table.

items.explain: Trace tables are used in GCSE exams and to find logic errors.
items.hook: **A trace table is an action replay** of every variable.

items.prompt: In a trace table for a loop, when do you add a new row?

options.text: Each time a variable’s value changes
Only at the very end, when the loop has finished
options.feedback: Then you would miss the steps in between.

options.text: Only when something is printed to the screen
options.feedback: Track every change, not just output.

items.explain: Following every change is what makes a trace table reliable.
items.hook: **New value? New row.**
**The leftmost bit is worth −128**: 11111111 is −128 + 127 = −1.
items.example: Computers usually store negative whole numbers, like a freezer’s −18 °C setting, in two’s complement.

items.prompt: In sign and magnitude, the first bit shows the sign (1 = negative). What problem does this cause?

options.text: There are two zeros, and normal addition goes wrong
It cannot show positive numbers bigger than 1
options.feedback: A leading 0 means positive.

options.text: It needs 16 bits to store any number at all
options.feedback: It can use any number of bits.

items.explain: Two’s complement fixes both problems, which is why computers use it.
items.hook: **Sign and magnitude has +0 and −0**: two zeros, one too many.

items.prompt: In 8-bit two’s complement, what is the leftmost bit worth?
items.hook: **The top bit is −128**; the other seven bits are positive as usual.

items.prompt: One quick way to find −n in two’s complement is…

options.text: write n in binary, flip all the bits, then add 1
write n in binary, then put a 1 at the front of it
options.feedback: That is sign and magnitude.

options.text: write n in binary backwards
options.feedback: Reversing bits changes the number completely.

items.hook: **Flip the bits, then add 1.**
**SELECT fields FROM table WHERE condition**: what you want, where it lives, which rows.
items.example: An online shop’s price filter runs a query like SELECT name FROM Products WHERE price < 20.

items.prompt: In a database table, one row (all the data about one thing) is called a…
items.explain: Each record is one hero; each field is one piece of information, like strength.
items.hook: **Record = row = one thing; field = column = one detail about it.**
items.example: In a school register, each pupil is a record and date of birth is a field.

items.prompt: In a database table, one column (like “name” or “home”) is called a…
items.explain: Fields have a data type, such as text or integer.
items.hook: **Field = column**, like a heading in a spreadsheet.

items.prompt: What is a primary key?

options.text: A field that is unique for every record
The password needed to open the database
options.feedback: It is a field, not a password.

options.text: The first field in every table
options.feedback: It is a field that uniquely identifies records.

items.explain: Names aren’t safe as keys (two people can share a name), so tables often use an ID number.
items.hook: **Primary key = a unique ID**, like a passport number.
items.example: Your NHS number is a primary key: no two people share one.

items.prompt: Which SQL query lists the names of heroes from Athens?

options.text: SELECT name FROM Heroes WHERE home = 'Athens';
SELECT Heroes FROM name WHERE Athens;
options.feedback: SELECT the field FROM the table WHERE a condition.

options.text: FIND name IN Heroes = Athens;
options.feedback: SQL uses SELECT … FROM … WHERE.

items.explain: SELECT fields FROM table WHERE condition;
items.hook: **SELECT what, FROM where, WHERE which.**

items.prompt: What does SELECT * mean?

options.text: Select every field
Select only starred records
options.feedback: * is a wildcard meaning all fields.

options.text: Multiply the fields
options.feedback: In SQL SELECT, * means all.

items.explain: SELECT * FROM Heroes; shows the whole table.
items.hook: The star is a wildcard: **SELECT star means every field.**

items.prompt: In a star network, every device connects to a central switch. What is the main disadvantage?

options.text: If the central switch fails, the whole network goes down
If any one cable breaks, every device on it stops working
options.feedback: Only the device on that cable is affected.

options.text: Data collisions are constant
options.feedback: Switches send data only to the right device, so collisions are rare.

items.explain: Advantage: one broken cable affects only one device, and it is easy to add devices.
items.hook: **Star = a hub in the middle**: if the centre fails, everything fails.
items.example: Most home networks are stars, with the router at the centre.

items.prompt: Why is a mesh network very reliable?

options.text: Data can take another route around a broken link
It has only one cable, so less can go wrong
options.feedback: It has many connections.

options.text: It uses the strongest and most expensive cables
options.feedback: Reliability comes from the many routes, not the cables.

items.explain: The internet itself is a giant partial mesh.
items.hook: **Mesh = many routes**: one link breaks, take another.
items.example: Mesh Wi-Fi uses several units around a house that pass data between each other.

items.prompt: In a client–server network…

options.text: clients request services and servers provide them
every computer is equal and shares directly
options.feedback: That is peer-to-peer.

options.text: the server asks each client for its files
options.feedback: It is the clients that ask; servers answer.

items.explain: Most websites, email and school networks are client–server.
items.hook: **The client asks; the server serves.**
items.example: Streaming a video: your phone is the client, and the company’s computers are the servers.

items.prompt: What is a MAC address?

options.text: A unique number in a device’s network hardware
An address given to a device by the router
options.feedback: That is an IP address, which the router hands out; a MAC address is built into the network hardware.

options.text: A website address typed into the browser
options.feedback: Web addresses are URLs.

items.explain: IP addresses can change when you move network; the MAC address is built into the hardware (though many phones now show each Wi-Fi network a disguised “private” MAC address for privacy).
items.hook: **MAC sticks to the machine; IP changes with the place.**
items.example: Your laptop gets a different IP address at school and at home, but its network card keeps the same MAC address.

items.prompt: Put the four layers of the TCP/IP model in order, from the top (nearest the user) down.
items.explain: Application (HTTP, email), transport (TCP: splits data into packets and checks they arrive), internet (IP: addressing and routing), link (the physical network: Wi-Fi, Ethernet).
items.hook: **All Teachers Inspire Learners**: Application, Transport, Internet, Link.
items.example: Watching a video: the app asks (application), TCP splits it up (transport), IP routes it (internet), Wi-Fi carries it (link).

items.prompt: Why are network protocols organised in layers?

options.text: Each layer does one job and can be changed alone
To make the internet slower but safer from hackers
options.feedback: Layers are about organisation, not speed.

options.text: So each layer can use a different language
options.feedback: It is a design choice that makes networks easier to build.

items.explain: You can switch from Wi-Fi to cable (link layer) and websites (application layer) still work.
items.hook: **Layers are a team where each member has one job.**
items.example: Like posting a letter: you write it, the post office sorts it, the van carries it; none needs the others’ job.
